Latest Update: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A major newly introduced study has uncovered important differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces.
  • Some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact.
  • James McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A major newly introduced study has uncovered important differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces. Published in Nature Mental Health, the research is among the most extensive investigations yet into how face perception works in autism.

Some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact. They may also find it more difficult to remember faces or interpret facial expressions compared with neurotypical individuals. Scientists have spent decades investigating the brain activity behind these differences. In the early 2000s, for example, researchers at Yale reported that brain regions responsible for processing faces highlighted lower activity in autistic individuals than in people without autism.

James McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity. Previous EEG studies, however, have typically examined signals from limited regions rather than analyzing activity across the entire scalp.

Recent findings suggest that to gain a more complete picture, McPartland and his colleagues conducted a study involving approximately 400 autistic children, examining electrical signals recorded across the scalp. They discovered that brain activity associated with face recognition was less clearly distinguishable in autistic participants. They also identified a striking difference in development: In neurotypical children, the brain's response to faces became more specialized with age, while autistic children did not show the same pattern.

"This is the first time we've leveraged the full volume of very rich information provided by an EEG recording to understand face perception and autism," McPartland claims.

How Scientists Discovered Differences in Autistic Brain Activity.

McPartland compares traditional approaches to studying face recognition with attempting to understand traffic throughout an entire city by monitoring just one downtown street.

"That's the way most research on face processing so far has worked," McPartland notes.

The new approach provides a much broader perspective, similar to observing traffic across an entire city using satellite imagery. To investigate these patterns, the researchers analyzed information collected through the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT). The dataset included autistic and neurotypical children across different age groups.

During the experiments, participants viewed pictures of faces and everyday objects while EEG equipment recorded their brain activity. Instead of concentrating on a small number of recording locations, the scientists examined electrical signals from all 128 electrodes positioned around each participant's scalp.

They then applied machine learning techniques to determine whether patterns in the recordings could reveal what each child was viewing.

The results indicated that brain activity provided a clearer indication of face viewing in neurotypical children than in autistic children. In other words, the electrical signals associated with seeing faces were less distinguishable in the autistic group.

"The neural activity that we measure at the scalp is just not as distinct in autistic children," states first author Jason Griffin, PhD, assistant professor of psychology at University of Houston. Griffin previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in McPartland's laboratory.

Industry observers note that the researchers also found that the ability to identify what a child was viewing from brain activity improved with age among neurotypical participants. This age related improvement was not observed in autistic children, suggesting that their neural responses to faces develop along a different pattern.

"Their face-specific processing is not following the same trajectory," Griffin claims.

Face Recognition Differences May Begin Earlier Than Previously Thought.

Beyond identifying differences in brain activity, the study offers latest insight into how early those differences emerge during face perception.

Recent findings suggest that recognizing someone involves multiple stages of neural processing. The sequence begins when visual information enters the eyes and continues as the brain interprets that information until a face is recognized.

It has been revealed that much of the earlier research on autism and face perception has concentrated on a brain signal called the N170. This measurable change in electrical activity typically occurs about 170 milliseconds after a person sees a face. Previous studies have shown that the N170 response tends to occur later in autistic individuals.

In a recent development, by analyzing brain activity over a wider period, the researchers found evidence that differences in face processing begin before this familiar signal appears. This suggests that autism related differences may arise at earlier stages of visual processing than researchers had previously established.

"But when you look at face processing through an approach that's more inclusive of the full temporal range of information, we're seeing that differences in autism occur even earlier," McPartland indicates.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Autism Diagnosis and Early Support.

The findings could eventually influence how researchers approach autism diagnosis and the development of supportive interventions.

According to recent reports, historically, some clinicians attempted to address difficulties with face perception by requiring autistic individuals to maintain eye contact. Research has since shown that forcing eye contact is not an effective solution. A better understanding of how face processing develops in the brain could help identify approaches that are more useful and appropriate.

It has been revealed that an ongoing challenge in autism research is separating neurological differences associated with autism itself from changes that may develop through the experience of living with the condition. According to the researchers, the patterns identified in this study suggest that differences in face processing are connected to underlying developmental characteristics of autism rather than simply reflecting accumulated life experiences.

"When we're seeing this expected refinement and specialization in non-autistic people, we're seeing a reduced developmental change in autistic people," McPartland explains.

Because the differences appear during development, the findings also raise the possibility that support aimed at helping autistic children interpret facial emotions could be particularly beneficial when introduced earlier in childhood.

However, the researchers emphasize that autism does not necessarily create difficulties that require intervention. Many neurodivergent people experience little or no impairment related to their autism and may neither need nor want additional support. For others, challenges with recognizing faces or understanding facial expressions can complicate everyday social interactions.

Sources indicate that "Imagine navigating life when it's hard for you to perceive the information in another person's face, from navigating a playground to navigating a job interview," McPartland notes. "This is one of the critical areas that causes difficulty for many autistic people.".

New Brain Signals Could Help Improve Autism Diagnosis.

Industry observers note that another potential application involves the search for more objective ways to assess autism. Presently, clinicians diagnose autism primarily by evaluating behavior because reliable biological tests are not yet available for routine diagnosis.

Scientists are investigating several possible biomarkers, which are measurable biological characteristics that could improve diagnostic assessments or help distinguish different groups within the autism spectrum.

It has been revealed that the newly identified patterns of face related brain activity could contribute to that effort. By examining how these neural signals differ among individuals, researchers may eventually develop additional diagnostic tools or better identify autistic people who are likely to benefit from particular forms of support, including social skills therapy.

Although more research is necessary before these findings can be used in clinical practice, the study provides a latest way to investigate how the autistic brain processes faces and how those responses change throughout childhood.

"This is a first step in introducing a new biomarker," McPartland says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, our lives are defined not by what we have but what we give — on what and whom we spend our energy and time, how we share our material possessions and our mental powers, what we do with our gifts. “Anything you do not give freely and abundantly becomes lost to you,” Annie Dillard wrote in contemplating the nature of creativity. “You open your safe and find ashes.”.

Paradoxically, the ability to give hinges on the ability to receive: You must be rested in order to labor, taking the repose it takes to recharge your vital energies; you must be interested in order to be interesting, taking the world in with a greedy curiosity that absorbs its beauty and strangeness in order to metabolize it into meaning.

C.S. Lewis (November 29, 1898–November 22, 1963) offers a wonderfully counterintuitive perspective on our notions of generosity and our ideas about what it means to be interesting in his memoir Surprised by Joy (public library).

With an eye to the ideal structure of the creative life, he writes:.

According to recent reports, it is a life almost entirely selfish. Selfish, not self-centred: for in such a life my mind would be directed towards a thousand things, not one of which is myself. The distinction is not unimportant. One of the happiest men and most pleasing companions I have ever known was intensely selfish. On the other hand I have known people capable of real sacrifice whose lives were nevertheless a misery to themselves and to others, because self-concern and self-pity filled all their thoughts. Either condition will destroy the soul in the end. But till the end, give me the man who takes the best of everything (even at my expense) and then talks of other things, rather than the man who serves me and talks of himself, and whose very kindnesses are a continual reproach, a continual demand for pity, gratitude, and admiration.

This is also why, Lewis intimates, the “thrill” of our greatest creative breakthroughs — those revelations that give us back to ourselves, out of which we give our best work to the world — is rooted in “self-forgetfulness”:.

Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else — whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard — does the “thrill” arise.

In a recent development, shut your mouth; open your eyes and ears. Take in what is there.

In a recent development, couple with John Steinbeck on the art of receiving, then revisit C.S. Lewis on what we long for in our existential longing.

How Positive Psychology Can Influence Public Policy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, imagine a medical doctor who never goes to the clinic and never publicizes availability for care.
  • It has been revealed that positive psychologists often act like that.
  • Recent findings suggest that while influencing public policy is not the only means to “do more,” it is (we believe) an undervalued avenue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, imagine a medical doctor who never goes to the clinic and never publicizes availability for care. Instead, the doctor provides care when close friends need help or when an emergency occurs in their presence. While these acts are good in and of themselves, one could not help but wonder whether the doctor’s approach maximizes their potential positive impact.

It has been revealed that positive psychologists often act like that. Like the doctor, we have specialized knowledge. We run studies and test theories. We accomplish things in our smaller circles. But without diminishing the value of these acts, one cannot help—as with our imaginary doctor—but wonder whether we could sometimes do more.

Recent findings suggest that while influencing public policy is not the only means to “do more,” it is (we believe) an undervalued avenue. Public policymakers are, to some degree, in need of the very thing we can (but often do not) provide.

It has been revealed that consider that public policy creators confront conflicting requests. Some voices ask for dismantling of camps for the unhoused, while others favor leniency. Some want programming to address the mental health of all schoolkids, while others worry these programs distract from education or may even be harmful. Others want more dollars for police enforcement while still others want less. Policy creators thus often want guidance. Absent guidance, they might follow their intuition or the most confident-sounding “researcher.” Psychologists can help.

Sources indicate that how best to help? In this piece, we briefly explore three ways that positive psychology can impact public policy.

Public officials often focus on brass-tacks issues such as better housing, education, transit, recreation opportunities, or public safety.

However, their impact on well-being is an implicit goal in almost all of those. People want better housing and transit so they can live happier lives. They want to be safe so that the subjective quality of their lives improves. Curiously, however, well-being is often omitted from formal discussion in policy procedures. It is everywhere and nowhere at the same time: It forms the backbone of almost every policy aim and yet is less often pursued in its own right.

Industry observers note that why is that? We suspect it is because the brass-tacks problems have measurable outcomes—and policymakers perceive that “well-being” is too ephemeral to be measured.

According to recent reports, that’s where psychologists, and perhaps especially positive psychologists, can help. Well-being no longer represents an unmeasurable ephemeral concept. The field has produced and refined legitimate scientific tools. Indeed, when we started in psychology, measures of personality and many other variables were well-established, but measures of well-being were treated with some suspicion. Since then, many studies have supported the value of well-being measures.

As a result, one way we as psychologists can improve public policy is to consistently remind policymakers that well-being can be measured just like housing costs or educational tests scores. Well-being measurement is not some elusive Platonic ideal—we can find well-validated tools that assess which factors facilitate flourishing along many dimensions, including hedonic, eudaimonic, physical health, and generic happiness (for a review of some, see our 2016 overview).

Thus, when policymakers turn to the academy for recommendations, we can put front and center our history of measurement of well-being. When studying the impact of a training program in a shelter for people who lack housing, psychological well-being of those receiving the treatment can be measured rather than measuring only items designed to facilitate well-being. Current public policy issues are often framed in well-being terms—and we have tools needed to provide policy recommendations. From the effects of artificial intelligence to social media usage, an array of studies exist showing the validity of our well-being tools in aiding policymakers.

One of us has often asked students to guess which psychological variables are most strongly associated with psychological well-being. None of the students have ever guessed “generalized trust,” even though trust consistently predicts well-being, with effects as large as many more widely known measures.

Recent findings suggest that indeed, generalized trust receives limited attention among academics (for exceptions, see some of the World Happiness Reports). Policymakers, too, often underestimate the importance of trust, so one way to influence policy is to remind policymakers of the importance of building trust in order to enable flourishing. Both general trust (e.g., “Do you think most people would return money to the owner if they found a wallet containing $200?”) and institutional trust (e.g., “Do you think the government can be trusted?” “Do you think corporations are corrupt?”) have surprisingly strong relations with well-being. Trust facilitates community, relations with neighbors, and conversations with strangers.

Industry observers note that misperceptions often create mistrust. For example, most people underestimate the proportion of others who act in trustworthy ways, as when most people underestimate how many individuals will return money found in lost wallets. Policymakers would be well-served to understand the difference between mistrust based on false perceptions and that which is at least partly justified, and psychologists are well-placed to help with that. Highlighting the trust findings can help policymakers focus on policies most likely to matter.

Industry observers note that sometimes those policies can focus on correcting misperceptions. Consider, though, what hurts trust among people. Mistrust can emerge when publicized incidents provoke fear; for example, if public spaces become truly more dangerous, then trust will decline.

Recent findings suggest that positive psychologists study three main topics: positive emotional states (i.e., well-being), positive traits (i.e., virtue and character), and positive institutions. Remember the third. Work with institutions. They help define your society.

Sources indicate that in our graduate studies, we received no training on collaborating with public institutions. A few strategies have helped us greatly:.

Their guide suggests, for example, that elected leaders and government administrators often won’t read even short written summaries of policy-relevant research that academics provide. However, those same leaders might:.

Initially, that sounded nonsensical to us, and disappointing after our many hours writing brief engaging summaries of research! Now, these recommendations are in accord with our observations. These interactions matter.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve also learned that government-funded institutions often have limited education budgets for their staff but want to do training. If you gain respect, they may be open to you providing training to their leaders. If you don’t present your conclusions, others, who might lack a scientific foundation, will present theirs.

Sources indicate that you can proceed with the confidence earned by well-validated science, but also mention qualifications or uncertainty. Policymakers often prefer simple answers, so social pressure discourages intellectual humility. Don’t let that preference for simplicity capture your thinking. We may be trusted more in the long run by presenting our data while admitting uncertainties or exceptions.

It has been revealed that let’s return to a medical metaphor. In medicine, if a prostate cancer test correctly identified 90% of men who have prostate cancer, but only 2% of men had prostate cancer, then the odds are that many positives would be false positives; in fact, most positives would probably be false positives.

That potential error does not disqualify the test—but ignoring the error would have bad consequences for everyone. Likewise, if our measures of well-being or measures of ill-being become widely used to screen students for further attention, we could recommend a test confidently and yet also need to continually remind users of the frequency of errors. Overdiagnosis could change student perceptions in unhealthy ways. Neglecting to emphasize the errors could harm people and undermine our credibility.

Adopt a strategy of confidence in the science while providing frequent reminders of necessary qualifications.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two weeks after an abbreviated edition of Art Basel Paris, the 29th edition of Paris Photo has taken over the Grand Palais (until 15 November), where digital art is enjoying a moment in the spotlight.
  • Recent findings suggest that the world of fine art photography is no stranger to controversies involving digital art, and it is heartening to witness the leading photography fair’s commitment to technological excursions within the medium.
  • This year, the digital sector is accompanied by a pedagogical exhibition programme titled Soft Photography, organised by the École Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne in Switzerland and devoted to contextualising the place of AI and CGI within photography.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks after an abbreviated edition of Art Basel Paris, the 29th edition of Paris Photo has taken over the Grand Palais (until 15 November), where digital art is enjoying a moment in the spotlight.

Recent findings suggest that the world of fine art photography is no stranger to controversies involving digital art, and it is heartening to witness the leading photography fair’s commitment to technological excursions within the medium. Featuring 12 exhibitors this year, the fourth iteration of Paris Photo’s digital sector has been curated by Marco De Mutiis of the Fotomuseum Winterthur, taking over from Nina Roehrs, who had helmed the first three editions.

This year, the digital sector is accompanied by a pedagogical exhibition programme titled Soft Photography, organised by the École Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne in Switzerland and devoted to contextualising the place of AI and CGI within photography. Spanning an interactive exhibition and talks, Soft Photography aims to offer some much-needed dialogue between the medium’s analogue and digital wings.

Paris Photo 2026 at the Grand Palais in Paris © Grégoire Grange.

The digital sector certainly contains some AI-generated imagery, such as New York- based Heft Gallery’s presentation of Alkan Avcıoğlu’s Disreality series, which is an expansion of the surreal landscape aesthetic he first introduced in a collaboration with Edward Burtynsky. But there are also plenty of analogue images throughout the sector, even photograms, enough to make one wonder just how much of a separate section this really is. A similar dynamic played out in the Zero 10 sector of Art Basel’s Swiss fair last June, where the term “digital art” was used so broadly that it begged the question whether a separate area was really warranted.

It has been revealed that noteworthy presentations at Paris Photo include the Venezuelan gallery Carmen Araujo Arte, which is showcasing Alejandro Cartagena’s mosaic-cut collages. Created from found photographs, the series is a manual interpretation of how images are made by generative AI by gathering found pixels. The works ask timely questions about authorship while also, in a rather sweet, analog gesture, highlighting just how much our art-making inevitably differs from that of algorithmic processes. The results are genuinely magnetic and intimate.

Palo Gallery’s installation of works from the artist duo Adrea Orejarena and Caleb Stein’s American Glitch series interrogates simulation theory as well as the nature of our screen-filled reality. Oscillating somewhere between the tone of David Lynch’s series Twin Peaks and surveillance footage, the presentation is a highlight, particularly Glitch Typologies (2020-24), the seven-channel sequence of floating images projected on the walls of a 3m-by-3m glass cube, the projectors hanging on a rod at its core, reminiscent of CCTV cameras. At a time of growing cultural cynicism, Orejarena and Stein offer a welcome reminder that the intersection of photography and technology can be whimsical, conspiratorial and surprising.

Yumo Wu, Old Dream No.1, 2026 Courtesy the artist and Licheng Ling Projects.

Yumo Wu’s solo stand with Licheng Ling Projects spans AI and darkroom analogue manipulation, with the images interspersed in such a manner that technique—though it inspires a certain sense of wonder—becomes secondary to the impact of the image. It is perhaps the best example at the fair of a presentation that moves beyond our fixation with what might be real and how it may have been created, with the artist instead asking her audience to quietly behold the images’ abstract textures. Wu is an emerging artist whose skill and willingness to experiment drowns out the noise, and the results are rather wonderful to behold. In addition to the stand marking her first solo presentation in Europe, one of her images is included in Paris Photo’s selection marking the bicentennial of the invention of photography.

Vincent Fournier, Orchis nubigena [Kunminga Gemina], 2026 Courtesy of the artist and Au Cube.

In a recent development, vincent Fournier’s Flora Incognita, presented by Au Cube, features large-scale portraits of speculative flowers derived from existing flora and manipulated to depict what may happen to them on another planet, exposed to different kinds of radiation or gravity. The photos may at first register as AI-generated images, but were in fact created with CGI using Houdini, a comparatively old-school software. Each image is presented in a wooden frame with a golden plaque on the bottom featuring the name of the plant, evoking the kind of 18th- or 19th-century botanical illustration that particularly benefits from the aesthetics of the Grand Palais, whose architecture harks back to a time of earnest scientific fascination and discovery.

In a recent development, the Upcoming York gallery Nguyen-Wahed’s solo stand devoted to the Los Angeles-based photographer Summer Wagner contains unframed, romantic, large-scale photographs featuring grainy, densely-textured and coolly-lit portraits. The presentation, only digital insofar as the images were shot on a digital camera, deals with our relationship with reality as "we’ve collectively succumbed to the tsunami or cultural and technological changes that have thrown image-making into an existential crisis”, according to the artist.

Summer Wagner, Blue Shift, 2024 Courtesy of Nguyen Wahed and the artist.

Meanwhile, facing the digital sector is Ruttkowski 68’s solo stand devoted to François Hallard’s large-scale Polaroid prints of flowers, with the title “Conversations avec Claude” written by the artist in bold letters at the top of the booth. On the second day of previews, Hallard added “(Monet) not IA” to the title, after countless visitors had presumed the works were related to AI. Evidently Anthropic’s AI engine has eclipsed one of the most consequential painters of the 20th century—at least in its claim to the first name Claude.

Sources indicate that given how much of an impact the nascent field of AI-generated photography has had on photography at large, it is unsurprising that we continue to add disclaimers and coin terms to differentiate the medium’s analogue lineage from its technological step-cousins. Several years ago, the dealer Howard Greenberg told me he favours the term “lens-based” to differentiate the two, and this seemed adequate at the time. But since then, plenty of artists (myself included) have incorporated photographic lenses, enlargers and other analogue tools and processes to experiment with and human-wash digital imagery, so “lens-based” may no longer be up to the task of distinguishing between an image taken with a camera and an image generated with a computer. “Synthetic photography” does have a nice ring to it, although the word itself makes one think of things like latex and carcinogenic sunscreen. Perhaps “soft photography” is the best term, for the moment.

Paris Photo’s digital sector and the Soft Photography programming deftly and quietly tackle the discipline’s ongoing existential crisis by demonstrating that digital art predates many of the technologies we are debating today, and its applications in contemporary photography today are legion.

Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain. Now, scientists have discovered that these painful episodes activate a surprising part of the brain, one closely connected to our sense of identity and how we think about ourselves.

It has been revealed that researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain. The discovery suggests that persistent back pain may become deeply intertwined with a person's sense of self, potentially helping explain why conventional pain treatments often provide limited relief.

Recent findings suggest that according to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. When pain persists for more than 12 weeks, it is considered chronic. For many patients, everyday movements can provoke sudden flare-ups that make an already difficult condition even harder to manage.

Although the brain plays a central role in how pain is experienced, researchers have struggled to identify the precise brain circuits responsible for pain triggered by movement.

Chronic Back Pain Activates the Brain's Sense of Self.

The new study, published on October 5, 2026, in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, identified an unexpected response involving the brain's Default Mode Network (DMN).

In a recent development, sometimes called the "self network," the DMN consists of interconnected regions in the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These areas are especially active when our attention turns inward, such as when we reflect on personal experiences, think about our identity, or consider our thoughts and emotions. In contrast, the network generally becomes less active when we direct our attention toward something happening around us.

Sources indicate that the researchers discovered that sudden back pain caused by movement switched this network on rather than off. This unusual response suggests that chronic pain involves more than the processing of physical sensations. It may also engage the brain systems that shape how people experience themselves.

In a recent development, the findings could help researchers understand why treatments that focus primarily on suppressing pain symptoms do not always work well for chronic low back pain. They also raise the possibility that targeting the DMN could offer a different approach to treatment.

Brain Scans Reveal a Surprising Difference Between Chronic and Acute Pain.

To investigate what happens in the brain during a pain flare, the researchers recruited 114 patients with chronic low back pain.

Industry observers note that each participant completed a "leg raise test," a standard clinical procedure used to provoke back pain. During the test, researchers monitored changes in brain blood flow using a specialized functional MRI method called arterial spin labeling. This technique allows scientists to track patterns of brain activity by measuring blood flow without relying on an injected contrast agent.

The team also examined how participants responded to a separate painful stimulus. They applied a harmless but uncomfortable heat sensation to the calf, similar to the brief pain someone might experience when accidentally touching a hot stove.

Comparing these two situations revealed a striking difference.

In a recent development, when movement triggered a flare of chronic back pain, the DMN became more active. However, when participants experienced the painful heat stimulus, the same network became less active, following the brain's typical response to acute pain.

The researchers also identified several other vital patterns:.

Together, these findings provide fresh evidence that chronic pain flares involve brain processes associated with personal identity, not just the physical experience of pain.

Why the Brain Reacts Differently to Chronic Pain.

During ordinary acute pain, the brain generally reduces activity in the DMN so it can concentrate on the immediate source of danger. This response helps shift attention away from internal thoughts and toward an external threat.

But the UC San Diego researchers found that movement triggered chronic back pain produced the opposite effect.

According to recent reports, "In every pain study, when you're experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates," mentioned corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, PhD, professor in the Department of Anesthesiology, endowed professor at the Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion, and director of the Pain Health and Mindfulness Laboratory at UC San Diego School of Medicine. "What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are.".

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that chronic back pain can become closely connected with the brain's internal representation of the self. Rather than processing pain solely as a physical warning signal, the brain may also link it to personal memories, expectations, and emotional experiences.

Sources indicate that for someone living with chronic pain, this means the experience can extend far beyond the moments when the pain is physically present. Worry about the next flare, memories of previous episodes, and fear of movements that might trigger pain can all become part of everyday life.

"The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It's contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain.".

This connection between pain and personal identity may help explain why chronic back pain can be especially difficult to treat.

A New Direction for Chronic Back Pain Treatment.

Because movement-triggered chronic back pain engages different brain networks from ordinary acute pain, researchers believe traditional treatments may fail to address some of the processes that sustain the experience of chronic pain.

Medications such as opiates primarily target pain signaling, but they may not adequately address the brain networks involved in the emotional and personal dimensions of persistent pain.

Recent findings suggest that "Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that's not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one's identity.".

The discovery points toward treatments that address not only the sensation of pain but also the brain's relationship with that sensation.

Recent work by Zeidan and his colleagues has explored two potential approaches: mindfulness meditation and the psychedelic compound psilocybin.

Both approaches are being investigated for their ability to help people experience physical pain without allowing it to become as closely tied to their identity. Early findings suggest that changing this relationship may reduce pain intensity, although additional research is needed to confirm the results and determine how effective these treatments may be.

"These types of mind-body and psychedelic medicine approaches target the whole person," Zeidan stated. "Mindfulness is a meditation technique that's about cultivating non-judgmental awareness of the present moment that dramatically reduces pain in a very unique way. Psilocybin seemingly resets the pain system that integrates trauma, past experiences and future worries to facilitate a restart, if you will. They're not a silver bullet -- you're not necessarily getting rid of the pain, but you're changing the relationship you have with that pain so it doesn't contaminate your everyday life.".

Can Mindfulness and Psychedelics Change How the Brain Experiences Pain?

Rather than attempting to eliminate every pain signal, these approaches aim to change how the brain interprets and responds to the experience.

Recent findings suggest that mindfulness meditation encourages people to observe their thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations without immediately judging or reacting to them. Psilocybin, meanwhile, is being studied for its potential to alter brain processes that connect pain with earlier experiences, emotional distress, and expectations about the future.

The goal is not necessarily to remove pain altogether, but to reduce how much it influences a person's thoughts, emotions, and daily functioning.

Zeidan's laboratory is at the moment conducting several clinical trials using brain imaging to investigate whether mindfulness meditation and psychedelic treatments can change the neural processes involved in self-reflection. Researchers hope to determine whether these approaches can reshape brain activity and improve how people subjectively experience chronic pain.

Although the research remains at an early stage, the findings offer a different way to think about persistent back pain. Understanding why the brain connects chronic pain with a person's sense of self could eventually help scientists develop treatments that address aspects of pain that conventional therapies often miss.

Additional study authors from UC San Diego School of Medicine include Morgan Gianola, Jon Dean, Conan Chen, Daniel Barrows, Gabriel Reigner, and Thomas Liu.

Funding was provided in part by the National Institutes of Health's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (Grant #R01AT009693) and the UC San Diego Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion. The researchers reported no conflicts of interest.

How Ideas of Masculinity Might Affect a Country’s Well-Being

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Internet has been awash in commentary in recent years on the topic of masculinity.
  • In the field of psychology, one way of thinking about masculinity is the notion of precarious manhood.
  • This may align with much of the messaging in the “manosphere,” and debates about it often consider the impact on individual boys and young men.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Internet has been awash in commentary in recent years on the topic of masculinity. It’s spawned an influx of podcasts and social media influencers—often referred to as the “manosphere”—that have attempted to define modern-day masculinity. The Netflix documentary Inside the Manosphere, hosted by British journalist and documentarian Louis Theroux, further ignited conversations as he unpacked the impact of manosphere influencers and their potentially harmful ideologies on young boys and men.

In the field of psychology, one way of thinking about masculinity is the notion of precarious manhood. As researchers Joseph Vandello and Jennifer Bosson explain, precarious manhood has three basic tenets: First, that manhood is an “elusive, achieved status, or one that must be earned”; second, that once achieved, this manhood status can be easily lost; and, third, that manhood is largely validated by others and requires demonstrations of proof.

This may align with much of the messaging in the “manosphere,” and debates about it often consider the impact on individual boys and young men. But what’s the broader impact on society? New research suggests that countries with higher precarious manhood beliefs fare worse in terms of their economies, health, and well-being.

A recent study published in Social Science & Medicine used data from the 2024 World Happiness Report (collected between 2021 and 2023), as well as data from an investigation of gender beliefs (over 33,000 college students across 62 countries from 2018 to 2020). The study’s authors, Boston College professor James Mahalik and Ph.D. candidate Michael Harris, focused on the 59 countries covered by both studies.

Industry observers note that precarious manhood was examined by asking respondents things like how easy it is for one to lose his status as a man and whether some boys never become men no matter how old they get. Happiness in the World Happiness Report surveys is based on the Cantril ladder: Respondents imagine a ladder, numbered from zero (the worst possible life) to 10 (the best possible life), and indicate where they personally feel like they stand on the ladder.

The researchers found that people living in countries with higher average precarious manhood beliefs tend to be less happy, while countries with lower precarious manhood beliefs tend to be happier. Lebanon and Nigeria are among the countries that have high precarious manhood beliefs and therefore low happiness. A number of Nordic countries, including Denmark, Finland, and Sweden, have low beliefs in precarious manhood and therefore high levels of happiness. The U.S. is in the mid-range for both precarious manhood beliefs and national happiness.

It may not come as a surprise to read these findings about Nordic countries, which are often categorized as more egalitarian, have more progressive gender norms, and frequently fall near the top of the World Happiness Report rankings. In the 2024 World Economic Forum Global Gender Gap Index, for example, Finland ranks no. 2 for gender parity, Sweden ranks no. 5, and Denmark ranks no. 15. Nigeria ranks no. 125 and Lebanon ranks no. 133 out of 146. The U.S. ranks no. 43. Mahalik and Harris speculate that countries with higher precarious masculine beliefs tend to be less happy because men require more validation of behaviors that emphasize domination and self-reliance.

Sources indicate that john Helliwell, one of the founding editors of the World Happiness Report, expressed a similar sentiment. “It’s in general true that happier societies are going to be ones where groups of people don’t feel under threat or challenged,” he noted. He also pointed out the social trust in Nordic countries, which has often been a distinguishing characteristic of cultures with harsher living conditions, where people are incentivized to cooperate because their survival historically depended on it.

In their recent study, Mahalik and Harris also found that countries with higher levels of precarious manhood beliefs had lower gross domestic product (GDP). They propose that in countries where masculinity is thought of as precarious, men may be discouraged from participating in fields that are critical yet perceived as feminine, like caregiving and education, and that such beliefs may also restrict women’s opportunities in the workforce—relegating women to fields considered feminine or restricting them from the workforce altogether. However, they note that lower GDP may be what fosters precarious masculine beliefs in the first place, as economic challenges could heighten fears about fulfilling the traditional masculine role of being a provider.

Other research finds different consequences for believing in this elusive and hard-earned version of masculinity. In a study of 62 countries by Vandello, Bosson, and other colleagues in 2023, they found that men in countries with higher precarious manhood beliefs had lower life expectancy by several years than men in countries with lower precarious manhood beliefs.

Why? There could be many explanations, but they also found that national precarious manhood beliefs predicted risky health behaviors, such as substance abuse, extreme sports, and reckless driving.

According to recent reports, mahalik, who’s been studying gender socialization since the early 1990s, mentioned there is longstanding research around the gender socialization of girls—more specifically, the messages they receive about body image, which research has linked to eating disorders. As Mahalik told me, “I’ve been interested in examining the messages that culture also gives to men, some of which are contradictory and inconsistent, and the impact of what men take in about their external valuation of worth.”.

While Mahalik’s and Harris’s study ultimately doesn’t prove that beliefs in precarious manhood cause lower national happiness, it raises important questions about the link between rigid masculinity norms and well-being. As researchers continue to examine what makes a happy nation, this upcoming study suggests that the answer may not just lie in government policy, but in how cultures interpret and frame masculinity. As Mahalik told me, “What sort of community are we creating if culturally we’re endorsing a model of masculinity in which men have to constantly guard against losing their status as men?”.

Spencer Spellman is a writer, editor, and photographer, with his writing and photography appearing in the Los Angeles Times, Condé Nast Traveler, AFAR, Sunset, Outside Magazine, Smithsonian Magazine, and Travel + Leisure.

The Relationship Between Comedy, Democracy, and AI

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (471 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust.
  • Humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification.
  • Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust.

Humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification. Humor is also fundamental to free societies, to freedom of thought, to democracy: To laugh together is to harmonize our deepest humanity.

Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence.

Sources indicate that in her altogether fantastic manifesto for breaking free from the prison of predictive technologies, Carissa Véliz argues that humor thrives in the same “spaces of indeterminacy” where creativity and innovation also thrive. (“Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous ‘I don’t know,’” the Polish poet Wisława Szymborska observed in her magnificent Nobel Prize acceptance speech.) With an eye to the emotional attunement of sharing laughter, Véliz considers the relationship between humor, democracy, and AI:.

According to recent reports, our sense of humor is a dialogue, and when we delegate the conversation to AI, we lose the personal relationship with another human being. Democracy itself is a conversation. If we give up our seat at that table and give it to an AI, we will lose our voice.

Industry observers note that comedy is not inconsequential for democracy. Comedy sets the tone for freedom. It gives us courage. A documentary about comedy clubs in war-torn Ukraine reminds me that humor is not a luxury; it’s indispensable. “When I went to Sarajevo to a film festival,” Cleese says, “people were talking about the early ’90s, when Yugoslavia was falling apart. Sarajevo is down in a valley, and the Serbs were up in the hills throwing shells down, and telescopic snipers were shooting people crossing the street. And they told me that they had found an underground car park, had turned it into a cinema, and they would show comedies, including Monty Python, and they would laugh. When they came out, an hour and a half later, they felt better. Nothing had improved. But they were better able to deal with their situation.” Comedy can be an ally in our challenge to defy the odds.

Recent findings suggest that humor, like creativity, works by defying expectation. It is a felicitous violation of the norm. Societies thrive and progress by continually challenging the norm, the given, the status quo. Every revolution, every change in regime, is the story of turning the old order from terrible to laughable.

How Paternity Leave Policies Help Moms, Babies, and Families

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1302 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When our second child was born, my spouse had several weeks of paternity leave under his parental leave policy at work.
  • According to recent reports, I’m a certified family life educator, and parental leave comes up regularly in my teaching and community work.
  • Still, I could not have imagined how significantly his leave would end up affecting our family and our connections with community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When our second child was born, my spouse had several weeks of paternity leave under his parental leave policy at work.

According to recent reports, I’m a certified family life educator, and parental leave comes up regularly in my teaching and community work. So I was aware of the benefits his leave could have for our family—in theory.

Still, I could not have imagined how significantly his leave would end up affecting our family and our connections with community.

In a recent development, during his leave time, my spouse took our oldest child to playdates and birthday parties. He swiftly became connected with our small-town network of families with kids close in age. I witnessed my spouse becoming more comfortable being the “main” parent in public, going to kid-centered community events, and connecting with other parents.

Our family is still seeing the benefits of those few weeks 10 years later.

Leave for supporting parents after the birth of a child isn’t standardized or required by law in most places in the U.S. Even countries with generous paid time off for the birthing parent don’t always offer similarly generous time for the non-birthing parent.

This diversity in leave policies can make it hard to assess the impact of leave for the non-birthing parent. But existing research suggests that extended leave for birthing parents and moderate leave for non-birthing partners positively impact infant well-being and reduce postpartum mental health challenges.

Leave for both parents with the birth of a child can significantly benefit parental mental health overall and maternal mental health specifically. Paternity leave assists in the mother’s recovery and contributes to less of an increase in stress and depression than for mothers whose partners didn’t take leave.

One Swedish study indicated that flexibility within paternal leave policies, such as allowing new dads to take intermittent time off after the birth of a child, helped reduce the incidence of maternal postpartum health complications.

It has been revealed that children also benefit from paternity leave. When a father takes significant leave—meaning at least two weeks—children report experiencing more father-child closeness and better communication in the relationship up to nine years later. And overall child health tends to improve when fathers take paternity leave.

Recent findings suggest that when paid leave policies are available for both mothers and fathers, breastfeeding is more likely to last longer. Longer breastfeeding is strongly linked to overall infant health and decreased infant mortality.

Allowing both parents to have sufficient time off to bond and adjust to their new roles can also have longer-term benefits within the family unit and contribute toward more equity in child rearing. Even in 2026, mothers are often considered the “default” parent, with fathers taking a more secondary role.

While fathers are more involved now than in previous generations, mothers are still more likely to be the first call from school. And even with an involved father, mothers continue to carry the invisible mental load of the family, an unseen burden of data, obligations, and preemptive planning tasks. This overreliance on mothers comes with a price: Mothers report being more stressed and tired than fathers do.

Industry observers note that as I experienced in my own family, when fathers have ample time off, it sets up the dynamic to be more balanced between parents. This helps reduce the strain on recovering mothers and redistributes some of the care work that goes into raising children.

It has been revealed that what’s more, paid leave policies have been shown to help families’ financial health. Pay rates during leave can vary widely depending on your company, organization, or country. Without full or close to full pay, many families cannot afford to take leave.

In the U.S., for example, the Family and Medical Leave Act allows time off, but not in all circumstances, nor is that time required to be paid. Many families cannot afford to take the full allowable time off, using up sick or vacation time if available. Many parents in the U.S. end up going back to work sooner than seems healthy.

Sources indicate that fresh parents in the U.S. often find themselves in an economic bind—they can’t afford to take leave, nor can they afford to rely on a single income to have a parent stay home. But many also can’t afford the child care rates for newborns, which tend to be particularly high. National averages for infant care at child care centers are nearly $200 more per month than toddler care. While rates vary significantly depending on where you live and what type of care you choose, infant care remains the most expensive.

Industry observers note that despite the lack of a paid U.S. federal leave policy for parents, both domestic and multinational companies have noticed that their workers care about parental leave policies. Some have begun to offer leave for supporting parents in order to recruit and retain workers.

U.S. leave policies consistently rank at or near the bottom when compared with other similarly developed countries, like the 38 members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

Recent findings suggest that some countries follow a “use-it-or-lose-it” model of parental leave, where fathers in particular are encouraged to take a more substantial role in child care. Sweden and Norway, for example, earmark 90 days of leave for each parent, and it cannot be transferred to or split with the other parent. This encourages both parents to take time off.

There are many options across countries with parental leave policies. Flexibility and defined expectations seem to be key contributors to getting the most out of the parental leave that is offered.

In a recent development, when non-birthing parents are men, another barrier to taking leave is the perceived social acceptability within their communities. Even when paid paternity leave is available, many men struggle to take it because of how traditional gender roles and expectations of masculinity frame child care as women’s work.

To offset these kinds of social pressures, countries like Japan and Austria offer incentives such as bonus leave time for families when fathers actually take their available leave. Germany offers a similar bonus, and it has found improved couple relationship satisfaction when fathers take more of their leave time.

Beyond improvements in maternal and infant health, both parents taking leave can create a more equitable workplace environment. Disparities and discrimination that come when only women take leave after birth can lessen when fathers and other supporting parents also take leave. Childbearing women are then less likely to be penalized, formally or informally, for taking parental leave.

Paid parental leave policies that provide leave for all parents, regardless of gender, also can help reduce structural inequality in the workplace across race and class. In the U.S., Hispanic and Black workers often have less access to paid leave policies and may experience increased pressure to return to work earlier than their white counterparts.

Recent findings suggest that as more states, countries, and corporations adopt more flexible and inclusive leave policies, researchers will continue to learn how parental leave benefits both parents and children. What they’ve found so far leads me to believe that, just like we’ve seen with prenatal care and early education programs, parental leave will prove to be an early investment in healthy children and families that pays dividends in the long term.

ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.

Dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds. In the Bistro night scene, standard three.js under WebGL leaves the cobblestones cool and flat, with a blown-out white hotspot around the round shop sign. Even with WebGPU and SSGI turned on, the lamp glare stays harsh and the pavement loses multi-bounce warmth. Slide the divider across to ThreeRT, and warm golden light spills from the shop window across the facade while overhead string lights tint the street in their own colors.

According to recent reports, the Zero-Day sci-fi corridor reveals an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline. On the three.js side, ceiling pipes and glossy floors pick up heavy speckle noise, and unlit industrial housings sink into dark blue shadows. ThreeRT keeps those white and grey panels legible through soft indirect bounce light from tiny amber emitters. It doesn't rely on light probes or baked maps, so moving the camera at 60 fps never breaks the reflections of off-screen geometry.

Sources indicate that that matters for the future of ray tracing in the browser. Today, ThreeRT runs its Rust and wgpu path tracer inside a native client while exposing a familiar three.js-style TypeScript API. The same scene code still runs as plain three.js in any browser or WebView, which gives developers one codebase across both worlds. As WebGPU hardware ray tracing matures on the web, that gap is closing fast.

According to recent reports, you can see the range in the project gallery, from the OpenStrikeRT foundry hall where a furnace lights the surrounding concrete, to smaller studies like Jeweller's Window, Daylight Home, and Boutique Showroom. Each surface reacts to real emitters instead of faked ambient fill. See the full project on ThreeRTâs website.

Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain.
  • Sources indicate that although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain.
  • After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Sources indicate that although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

"The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," indicates Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake.".

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow.

The study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

It has been revealed that the latest findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Recent findings suggest that cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an crucial indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain.

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

Industry observers note that to examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

It has been revealed that the team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

Recent findings suggest that "Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," indicates Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance.".

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study.

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

Industry observers note that the study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

Funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.

  • In a recent development, when two people have loved one another, each has become embedded in the marrow of the other’s being and both have had a profound experience that cannot be unhad even when the slender thread of grace between them is severed, by death or disenchantment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

To love is to sign a contract with loss. To love anyway is both the great tragedy and the great triumph of life.

In a recent development, when two people have loved one another, each has become embedded in the marrow of the other’s being and both have had a profound experience that cannot be unhad even when the slender thread of grace between them is severed, by death or disenchantment. “No one you love is ever dead,” Hemingway wrote in his moving meditation on death and the meaning of life disguised as a letter of consolation to a bereaved friend.

According to recent reports, death, of course, is only one species of loss, one way our loved ones can leave us. We can also be left in life, left behind, left wondering where love goes when it goes. At its most discomposing, abandonment can feel like a living death.

All deep loss has one thing in common: It opens an absence so acutely felt it kidnaps us from presence, takes us away from our own lives and their insistent, inconvenient, sacred ongoingness. In memory or in fantasy, we end up refugees from reality, ceding the only thing that is ever ours for the keeping: the living moment. In all missing, we miss life.

That is what the achingly missed Wendell Berry (August 5, 1934–August 31, 2026) explores in this gasp of a poem, originally published in the November 17, 2025 issue of The Newly introduced Yorker:.

THE LOVED ONES by Wendell Berry.

The loved ones we call the dead depart from us and for a while are absent. And then as if called back by our love, they come near us again. They enter our dreams. We feel they have been near us when we have not thought of them. They are simply here, simply waiting while we are distracted among our obligations. At last it comes to us: They live now in the permanent world. We are the absent ones.

Couple with physicist Richard Feynman’s extraordinary love letter to his wife written long after her untimely death, then revisit Wendell Berry on creativity and love and his timeless antidote to despair.

Breaking: How India Is Embracing Social-Emotional Learning
